draft.summary: Technicians discuss practical troubleshooting approaches and common failure points for VRV and VRF systems. Key topics include reviewing error histories, checking sensor faults, and diagnosing failed control transformers.
draft.safety: Always disconnect and verify electrical power is off before inspecting internal controls and transformers.
steps: Ask on-site facility personnel about previous error history and part replacements.
Check error codes on central controllers, outdoor units, or manufacturer apps.
Perform a visual inspection for oil stains indicating refrigerant leaks.
Connect gauges and record baseline operating parameters before seeking technical support.

draft.title: Understanding Class 2 Equipment and 2-Core Cables
draft.summary: This video explains why some appliances use two-core flexible cables without an earth conductor. It demonstrates how to check appliance rating labels for the double-insulated symbol.
draft.safety: Ensure appliances are completely unplugged and isolated from electrical power before opening plugs or fittings.
steps: Open the ceiling rose to inspect two-core flex wiring.
Examine a standard plug showing line, neutral, and protective earth conductors.
Open a two-core plug to verify absence of an earth conductor.
Check the appliance rating label for safety certification symbols.
Identify the square-in-a-square symbol indicating Class 2 double-insulated construction.
Confirm that Class 2 appliances do not require a protective earth connection.
draft.subject: Fundamentals

review.reason: Clear explanation of Class 2 double insulation and when earth conductors are not required on plugs.

draft.title: Rolling Walls Without Leaving Lap Marks
draft.summary: This video demonstrates how to roll interior walls smoothly without leaving lap lines, flashing, or hatbanding. It explains the importance of maintaining a wet edge, loading the roller properly, and laying off the paint.
draft.safety: Ensure adequate ventilation in indoor work areas to prevent buildup of paint fumes.
steps: Cut in edges and roll before the perimeter paint dries.
Fully load the roller sleeve with paint to prevent dry rolling.
Overlap each roller stroke by fifty percent over the wet paint.
Maintain a consistent wet edge across the entire wall section.
Lay off the finish evenly with light top-to-bottom roller passes.

queue.title: How to Replace a Broken Sprinkler Head | Mower Damage Repair | Sprinkler Warehouse
queue.description:
In this video:
• Dig out the damaged sprinkler and expose its connection.
• Choose the correct head, nozzle, and fitting.
• Use a swing joint to make height adjustments easier.
• Flush out dirt and debris before putting the sprinkler into service.
• Set the head at soil level and firmly pack the dirt around it.
• Check the spray direction, arc, and watering distance.

Whether you’re replacing a rotor, spray head, or spray body with a rotary nozzle, matching the sprinklers on your zone helps maintain consistent watering.

draft.title: Replacing a Damaged Lawn Sprinkler Head
draft.summary: This video demonstrates how to excavate, select, and replace a damaged pop-up sprinkler head. It also covers using swing joints to set the head flush with the soil grade and flushing lines before final installation.
draft.safety: Ensure the irrigation system is depressurized before digging and be mindful of buried cables or pipes.
steps: Dig out the soil around the damaged sprinkler to expose the fitting.
Select a matching replacement head, nozzle, and adjustable swing joint.
Flush the water line briefly to clear dirt and debris.
Thread the new sprinkler head onto the fitting at soil grade level.
Backfill the excavation and pack soil firmly around the body.
Adjust the nozzle arc and spray direction to match the zone coverage.
draft.subject: Sprinkler Head Replacement

review.reason: Provides clear, practical instructions on replacing broken sprinkler heads and adjusting height to prevent future damage.
unsafe: Working in soil and handling tools without work gloves

draft.title: Understanding BW and CW SWA Cable Glands
draft.summary: This video explains the differences between BW indoor and CW outdoor steel wire armoured cable glands. It details every component included in a gland pack and how to select proper sizes using selection charts.
draft.safety: Ensure cables are completely isolated and wear gloves to protect hands from sharp steel wire armour edges.
steps: Identify BW glands for dry indoor use and CW glands for damp outdoor environments.
Inspect the pack to confirm it contains shrouds, earth rings, and gland assemblies.
Check the manufacturer chart to match cable core count and conductor size.
Disassemble the gland into the locknut, gland body, and gland or sealing nut.
Trap the steel wire armour securely against the gland body cone.
Tighten the locknut and slide the protective shroud over the finished joint.

draft.title: Stripping Cables Using Side Cutters
draft.summary: This video shows how to score and remove the outer PVC sheath of a flexible cable using diagonal side cutters. It also demonstrates how to apply correct pressure to strip conductor insulation without damaging fine copper strands.
draft.safety: Ensure cables are completely de-energized and verified safe before cutting or stripping.
steps: Position the side cutters around the outer PVC cable sheath.
Nibble gently around the outer sheath without cutting the inner conductor insulation.
Bend the cable to snap the scored sheath and slide it off.
Apply controlled cutting pressure onto the individual core insulation.
Pull the cutters outward to remove insulation without severing copper strands.
draft.subject: Fundamentals

review.reason: Clear demonstration of fundamental hand-tool technique for stripping flexible cables without damaging conductors.
